# Enjoyment when competing against believed-human versus known-computer opponents: a map of the empirical studies (as of 2026-01-27)

## Executive Summary

Only a small core of studies directly compares a believed or known human opponent with a computer opponent in a competitive game while measuring enjoyment-related constructs. The clearest cases are an fMRI study in which a tank-shooter game was played against alleged human and computer opponents: ventral striatum activity tracked self-rated pleasure, and vmPFC and dorsal striatum responded more to winning against a human [1]. Two psychophysiology publications [2][3] compared a computer, a friend and a stranger as opponents and reported more positive emotion, presence and engagement against humans. A Call of Duty experiment told players the same agent was either an agent or an avatar and measured arousal [4]. A study of rock-paper-scissors played against a believed human, a humanoid robot or a random computer reported engagement-like brain activity ordered human > robot > random [5]. Behavioural-engagement outcomes appear in a study of re-challenge decisions after defeat by an AI or a believed human, with a mixed result across three experiments [6]. Rehabilitation-game studies compare human competition with playing alone against the computer, using the Intrinsic Motivation Inventory [7][8].

Designs fall into three families: psychophysiology and self-report in commercial video games, neuroimaging with simple matrix games (rock-paper-scissors, matching pennies, card guessing), and exergame or rehabilitation studies. Outcomes are mostly presence, arousal and mentalizing; explicit enjoyment, flow and motivation are less often the primary outcome. Several candidate records had no abstract, so their inclusion rests on title only. The gateway call cap (60) was reached before every planned query ran, so the list is probably incomplete. No replications or direct contradictions were found, and the evidence is dated (mostly 2002–2017).

## Introduction

Question: which original studies compare competing against a believed-human opponent with competing against a known-computer opponent, in competitive games, with enjoyment-related outcomes (self-reported enjoyment, emotional valence, motivation, flow, behavioural engagement, neural reward)? T is 2026-01-27; only documents dated before T were used. English-language journal or proceedings papers were eligible, and identical experiments counted once. Plugin: cs-ai (the nearest available; no plugin covers games psychology, so its engines OpenAlex, Crossref, Europe PMC and dblp were used). Method: seven searches over two waves (four on distinct angles, three on chaining and new vocabulary), a batch read of abstracts for the uncertain candidates, then a report and a verification pass.

Assumptions. (1) Studies where the opponent is a real human, with no belief manipulation (friend vs stranger vs computer), are kept as borderline because the human-versus-computer contrast is the same in effect; if the criteria require a belief manipulation, these would drop out. (2) Neuroimaging studies with mentalizing outcomes but no explicit reward or affect measure are listed as borderline foci. (3) Economic games with no competitive-game framing were excluded.

## Main Analysis

### Finding 1 — Self-report and psychophysiology in video games favour human opponents, but most contrasts use real humans

The most direct evidence comes from three video-game studies. In a competitive tank shooter, an fMRI study used alleged human and computer opponents; ventral striatum activation was associated with self-rated pleasure, and vmPFC and dorsal striatum responses to winning were stronger against a human [1]. Ravaja and colleagues compared playing against a computer, a friend and a stranger with self-report, heart interbeat intervals and facial EMG, and found higher presence and engagement and more positive emotional responses against humans [2]. A follow-up with non co-located opponents used EMG, interbeat intervals and skin conductance and reported more positive emotion, arousal, presence and engagement against a human; its abstract speaks of the "mere knowledge of who is controlling the opponent character" [3]. A 2008 paper on online games against computer- versus human-controlled opponents lists presence, flow and enjoyment in its title, but only the title was available [9].

What qualifies this: in [2] the abstract does not state whether participants were deceived or were simply paired with real humans, so the "believed human" criterion is not established; [9] is judged on its title alone. A Call of Duty study with twenty players used the same agent in both matches, told as agent or avatar, and found arousal differences when the enemy was first encountered, with mixed measures later and some players not convinced of the opponent's humanity [4]. Two Wii-based and strategy-game papers on human versus computer opponents report physiological or cognitive-load outcomes; the Wii Boxing study found no difference in heart rate or oxygen consumption between opponents [10], and the strategy-game study (title only) targets cognitive load [11]. Eastin's study found that a human rather than computer opponent increased aggressive thoughts, with presence as the other outcome [12].

Consequence: the strongest enjoyment-specific evidence rests on one fMRI study [1] and two physiological publications from the same research tradition [2][3].

### Finding 2 — Neuroimaging studies are the largest cluster, mostly on mentalizing rather than reward

Several fMRI/PET studies manipulate belief about the opponent in simple games. A PET study had volunteers believe they played stone-paper-scissors against the experimenter or against a computer, while the opponent actually produced a random sequence; only anterior paracingulate cortex was more active under the intentional stance [13]. An fMRI rock-paper-scissors study used a believed human, a humanoid robot with AI, and a computer playing randomly; activity for the artificial agent was larger than for random but lower than for human in several attention and executive regions, "supporting the intrinsically engaging nature of social interactions", while medial prefrontal cortex and right TPJ responded to the human only [5]. A competitive game with gains and losses, reported as fMRI experiments, found a network sensitive to opponent type (human > computer) [14]. A matching-pennies study told participants they faced a human or a computer although the algorithm was the same, and found the opponent affected behavioural entropy, with anterior insula tracking entropy [15]. In a card-guessing game, a close friend, a confederate and a random number generator were the competitors; striatal responses were stronger for social than non-social competitors in an exploratory analysis [16]. A prisoner's-dilemma fMRI study with a computer, functional robot, anthropomorphic robot and human partner reported that participants experienced more fun and competition with increasing human-like features, with medial frontal and right TPJ activity rising accordingly [17]. Further studies compared humans with a computer in resource conflicts (more sharing with a human partner) [18] and compared a human, android, robots and a computer in matching pennies [19].

Qualification: the outcomes are mostly neural correlates of mentalizing, not reward or enjoyment; only [1] and [17] pair the opponent manipulation with pleasure or fun ratings, and [16] reports a reward-related striatal contrast with a non-social competitor. Several of these tasks are matrix or guessing games whose competitive framing is thin ([17] is an iterated prisoner's dilemma; [18] has a sharing option). Consequence: the neural literature shows a robust human-versus-computer difference in social-cognition regions but offers few direct reward-response contrasts. Verdict: probable for mentalizing differences (the robot study frames its result as "first evidence" [17]); open for reward.

### Finding 3 — Behavioural engagement and motivation: few studies, mixed results

Behavioural engagement is measured in three families. In three experiments (N = 74, 788 and 500), participants competed against an AI or believed they competed against a human in a logical-thinking task, and the number choosing to re-challenge did not differ between conditions in two experiments but was lower in the AI condition in the other [6]. Rehabilitation-game studies use the Intrinsic Motivation Inventory: a two-player air-hockey game compared single-player (against the computer), competitive (against a human) and cooperative modes in 30 unimpaired and 8 stroke participants; unimpaired participants preferred the two-player modes, and those who liked the competitive mode put in more effort [7]. A multisession study had participants play three sessions against a human opponent and then one against a computer; those who played against a friend or relative at home showed higher enjoyment and exercise intensity when competing, whereas pairs in the clinic showed no significant differences [8]. A study that asked participants about agent perceived agency told them they would play an online image-recognition game against a computer- or human-controlled opponent (always computer-controlled) and measured social presence, finding copresence higher against a computer-controlled than a presumed human-controlled opponent in one condition [20].

Qualification: in [7] and [8] participants know the identity of the opponent, so these are aware-human versus aware-computer contrasts, and in [8] "alone" is confounded with a solo task. The mixed pattern in [6] shows the human advantage is not universal. Exergame competition studies, such as a cycling race with heart-rate balancing, address competition but do not report a human-versus-computer contrast [21]. Verdict: open.

### Finding 4 — Moderators and neighbouring manipulations

Opponent characteristics other than identity were studied with deception designs that never compare human versus computer. A study told women they played against a male or female competitor who was actually an AI, and found opponent gender affected perceived stress and skill ratings [22]. A study of exergames varied opponent body size [23]. A study of same-gender human dyads compared emotions in cooperative and competitive play [24]. Bots trained to play like humans were preferred in a first-person shooter, a computer-versus-computer-design contrast without a human comparator [25]. A study of people defeated by AI examined causal attribution [6]. These are adjacent, not eligible, but show that the believed-opponent-attribute paradigm is widespread.

Consequence: the same cover-story method used for human-versus-computer contrasts has been applied to many other attributes, and the 2008 [17], 2012 [5] and 2014 [19] studies extend the contrast to robots, androids and anthropomorphic computers. Verdict: probable that agent human-likeness is a continuous moderator; no experiment isolates it for enjoyment.

## Synthesis & Insights

Taken together, the sources suggest that human opponents produce higher presence, arousal and positive emotion and stronger mentalizing activity. The effect on reward and enjoyment per se has the thinnest direct support [1][17]. This is my analysis: the research foci are (a) physiological emotion and presence, (b) mentalizing and social cognition, (c) motivation in exergames and rehabilitation, (d) behavioural persistence after loss. Designs differ widely in whether belief is manipulated through deception, a real human is used, or the opponent type is simply known. Almost all evidence predates 2018, apart from [6] and [20]; no large-scale or preregistered replication was seen.

## Limitations & Caveats

The gateway cap of 60 calls was reached during the second wave: four planned citation chains and six planned vocabulary queries (chess/poker, esports, VR avatars, bots in multiplayer, ventral striatum EEG) were not run. Several candidates (Weibel 2008, Lim & Reeves 2010, Kobayashi 2010, Chen 2015, Kubo 2014, Gajadhar 2008) had no abstract and are included or excluded on title only. Some included studies are borderline (real humans without belief manipulation; neural outcomes without enjoyment measure). Fewer than ten sources are fully read on abstract with a direct human-versus-computer enjoyment contrast, so the conclusions are provisional. No review published after T was opened.

## Recommendations

Re-run the missing chains (citing Weibel 2008 and the 2009 non co-located study) and the unrun queries with a higher call cap. Read full texts of the title-only candidates. For future primary work, combine a deception manipulation with validated enjoyment and flow scales and report manipulation checks.

## Methodology Appendix

Process: four searchers on seven angles (wave 1), then three in wave 2 (chaining, new vocabulary, neighbouring fields); wave 2 was cut short by the 60-call gateway cap, so the stopping rule was the ceiling, not saturation. Wave 1 produced about 12 eligible candidates; wave 2 produced new possibles (Chaminade 2012 and the neuroimaging cluster) which were settled by the free abstract batch of `read_possibles.py`. The plan of findings changed little (the neural finding was expanded).

Source coverage: active: OpenAlex, Crossref, Europe PMC, dblp; skipped or degraded: Semantic Scholar not wired (key S2_API_KEY, free registration); suggestions: none.

Verification: rule "verified = what carries a decision"; sentences of the findings not in the summary or a verdict were not checked (traceable by `[n]`). 51 claims checked: 46 FOUND, 2 DISTORTED, 1 ABSENT, 2 SOURCE-UNAVAILABLE. Removed: A48 (Finding 1 verdict sentence, ABSENT; no bibliography entry lost). DISTORTED corrected from the discrepancy, not re-verified: A41 (`[2]`, `[3]`, executive summary wording on number of studies) and A49 (`[17]`, Finding 2 verdict certainty). Kept unverified, SOURCE-UNAVAILABLE (no abstract): A14, A15 (`[9]`).

Biases looked for: preprint status (one preprint seen, excluded), single-run protocols, retractions (check run by the delivery tool).

Cost: about 60 gateway calls; 7 searchers; mode: standard. Machine annex files: card.json, result.json.

One-line summary: a small, mostly pre-2018 literature shows human opponents raise presence, arousal and mentalizing activity, with sparse direct enjoyment and reward evidence.
